speaker: Speaker 2

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Have you ever won any awards, honors, or ribbons, display at any county fairs?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: A lot of millions, but you know.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, okay. You've gotten ribbons and serious things?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Not so much here, but you know, throughout all of the time because here mostly they do it with the kids. And 4-H work, but we take things to this fair and we take them to the second fair.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What sorts of things are there? So, our livestock.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Most of the stuff in our garden, stuff in our beds. I used to take all of my sewing and cooking and things like that when I was in 4-H myself. What did they do? Most of the things were in connection with 4-H. Okay.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Does that take care of that? So, do you want to just go over that or you can just start telling about your lives? Okay.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I guess I would consider living in a rural area an advantage because I never lived anywhere else and I don't want to live anywhere else. If I wasn't happy about it, I would want, you know, perhaps might think about living somewhere else, but I don't. I think it's the only place to raise children. First, I said I don't want three teenage boys on the street. And it gives them lots of opportunities to be outside and to learn to work with their hands. And I have great hopes that if they learn to keep baby animals and things alive and feed things before they feed themselves, that they'll take better care of their families when they get up to the age where they'll have them. Rather than just hope it comes haphazardly.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Have they mentioned whether they would like to later live in a rural area?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Right now, they all say they wouldn't trade with anybody to live in town. And they all, I think probably would, because job opportunities don't exist. So, go look at that cow! Okay, got a cow that's going to have a calf right away. So I think that people, a lot of people who live in rural areas, they'll have to work much harder than the people who live in town. Because right now, under the pressure of paying, and we have to keep an eye on the cow. The coyotes got into our sheep last week. And then we have this huge garden and everything like that. It keeps you much more tied down and you have much, many fewer choices as to what you do with your time. And I have a dehydrator and I dry it too. I freeze more than I can.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What kind of dehydrator do you have?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: One of those electric four shelf ones. Works really well, I really like it. I got it last fall so I haven't used it as much as I will this year because I'll have it for the summer.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I'm going to try getting into that.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I think it's a good thing because you don't have to have the hot stuff.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is there any place we can record this?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Ross? We have to have a quieter so you move because it's not easier for us to.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I'm just afraid we'll pick up that. Right. You know.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Right. We don't want you tape recorded. Our family life here is almost identical to what it was when I was a child. There were four of us. We were almost exactly the same distance apart in ages. And we did a great many of the same things except when I was at home it was a dairy farm mainly. But we took the same kinds of things in 4-H and had a lot of the same opportunities and took music lessons and did basically the same things that we were doing with our children. There weren't very many differences there. We've never had any free time. It didn't matter where I lived. We got up and milked the cow and did all the regular routine things. There was never such a thing as to sleep in. And when my brothers and sisters and I were all in 4-H and the main way we got to see anything or do anything was through trips in 4-H and by achievements that way and earning trips and things to do.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you go on a lot of trips?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: At least I was on judging teams quite a bit of the time and would get to go to Boston which was a really big thing and I got to go to West Virginia to the Rural Youth Conference.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What did you think of Boston?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well it was a real big thing because Eastern Massachusetts and Western Massachusetts where we lived were very very different from each other in the way people talked. You've probably heard where the Kennedys talk and everything. Well people in our part of the state didn't talk that way or anything. So it was a really big thing and of course they had the subways and all the things we've never heard of. It was always a really big deal. We were expected to go to school. Not ever questioned it. My mother and father did not have an education but there was never ever any consideration almost as though you're predestined to go. There was just nothing. And everybody did.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You expect that of your children too?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: They're saving all their egg money and their milk money and things like that. They will be prepared as much as they can.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What do they do? Do they take care of the chickens and things?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And then the profits are theirs. Most of it income from sheep. One of them from milking a cow and one of them from eggs. And then when they sell their fat stock it's fair to them. There's profits from that. Same way that we did it. The things that are available in St. Mary's now were the things that were available when we had our children in the hospital. The way everything is now.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did your husband deliver your children at the hospital?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Right. Which was not the thing to do at the time.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Why didn't you do it then?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Because we wanted to. We didn't want to make wives. There was no law that you couldn't. It was just customary. The doctors didn't have to deliver their own wives and children.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Was it natural childbirth?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: At the time they had that stuff that you could strap onto your wrist that I did have in case it was necessary. I didn't have those Lamont's lessons or anything. But I had babies very, very easily. When I had one baby we'd go to the hospital as fast as we could go. So it was really no problem. I had two babies. It was never any big deal.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I can hear the vacuum cleaner turning off now. I can hear it approaching. I should never have a family with all of these things going on. I hate you interrupting your housework. You're not my family. I'm your sister.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We have all these things. But it's always like this. There's just no good time because if there isn't one thing there are three others. Because Thursday I have to take Kathy to the plant. Friday we're having the livestock thing down at the fairgrounds. It's for the whole county. And on Monday it was demonstration day in Columbus. I have a little kids and today it's for the big kids in St. Mary's. They're always on these things. But we wanted a large family. Now that we have boys who are 13, 14 and 15. You wonder if it was such a good idea occasionally. But we are surviving. I think I got my knowledge about all the children things probably basically from my mother. But then you get some of it from college and then when you teach school you learn a few things you don't want to let happen to your own.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I can believe that. When did you teach school?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: When I first came out here. I taught two years in seventh grade here and then I taught in Plummer for four years.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And when did you teach?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Here I taught English and history and all the related things. You know like spelling and social studies sort of things. And in Plummer, well it's such a small high school you teach almost everything also. So I taught English, United States history, biology, all the home ec courses, coach the basketball team. You know sometimes during the time. Because three of the years I taught over there there were no other women teachers so you had to do everything that had anything to do with the girls.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you like teaching?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Real well.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you plan on going back into it later?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Haven't ever considered it seriously because right now we just couldn't manage the time. And I had gone through with my class over there from freshman to seniors and they ended and I ended and it seemed like the time to end. And we had Todd so I just haven't ever. There's just no way you know except in case of emergency. I don't know how anyone could predict a future for children never mind grandchildren the way the world is moving right now.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well some of these questions are for you know different age ranges.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I hope that by preparing them to raise livestock and garden and to help me with all of the things that we do. With like preserving the vegetables and all of those things will help prepare them like I taught all of the boys how to sew and sewing machine and things. They'll be able to take care of themselves and be prepared to do that regardless of what comes up. And I know I talked to my mother about that because all of her other grandchildren are city children and whether it was realistic to be as rural as we are. She thought they had a better chance of adjusting probably than city children would be in case of calamities and upheavals and economic disasters or whatever there might be.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I think she's right. I really do.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: So that's what I'm like last year we had a real program on learning to grow absolutely everything that would grow in this area that we knew of and a few things that we experimented with. So they would feel you know try everything and maybe something will survive if there's a weather problem or we're also going to have that trouble this year too. The weather has been so unusual that they each have one fourth of the garden for their 4-H project and also to one of them is raising peanuts and we have all kinds of strange things down there.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: When did you plant the peanuts?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: They can't be planted according to the instructions and so it's very warm so we plant it in the end of May and then it got very very dry and it didn't come up good. So we don't know what we're going to have. We have 12 peanut plants.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I bought some peanuts back from Georgia and next year we're going to try.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well they're started. We have two okra plants. We have all kinds of spods and stuff. So regardless of anything supposedly something will grow up a tour and then you'll have it. We also have done a lot of companion planting. That's what Kent is doing his demonstration on this afternoon. We have a lot of plants that like each other and dislike each other and are natural insect repellents and double crapping and intercrapping and all that stuff. So we can cram everything in. We may not be able to walk in the garden but like the beans are all planted in with potatoes and everything is all crammed in. Probably completely totally all off from this thing. I better get back on my question. For recreation. That's kind of a bad question. We can never all get away at once.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you and your husband ever just get away by yourself?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We never have since we had children. Not even one time. Last year the kids all had to be gone at the same time for three days. That's the first time we had ever been in the house without them. We had never gone without them anywhere else either. We enjoyed it so much that this year we sent them all away for a week. It just turned out that everyone had somewhere to go and we arranged it for them all to be gone. It was terrible for the chores. It took me two hours every morning and two hours every night. It was so quiet and peaceful that we could just hardly believe it. We let it happen that way this year on purpose. In the April school vacation Mike took the two little ones to Disneyland. Ross you're getting noisy again. Why don't you play basketball?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Alright. I'm going to bring it back to my daughter.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Mike is going to take Ross to Canada in August for three days. We told him to each pick out something that would take three days and we would try to sandwich it in. But we don't think Todd is going to get his three days. He's the oldest one because he's already been to Washington DC on a 4-H trip to the national conference and he went all by himself which was quite the experience. Now he is at Fort Wright College in Spokane taking two weeks of debate training because he's on a high school debate team. So we think when he gets home he's going to have to work and catch up on other things. His choice was to go camping up in the woods somewhere. The forestry club will go for one overnight so that's just going to have to do it. Everyone else will have had their three days except I don't know when I'm getting mine. But last year in October I went to the University of Idaho with the debate team and she offered the girls for the debate coach. And that's the first time I had ever gone anywhere by myself like that. So we have been pretty much at home.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You didn't mention how you and your husband met.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I met him through 4-H. I knew him for a long time before we got married. We got married I guess because we wanted to.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Had you always thought about yourself as being married?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I always, maybe beforehand.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah beforehand. Had you always in your future seen yourself as being a married woman?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh yes, I was going to have six children.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: All those things. Right. But my life now is so much like my life was when I was growing up. There has really been no major change. It wasn't as though I dreamed of one thing and did something completely different. It was just sort of like one routine thing. Except in a different place but we lived in a valley. It just ran the opposite way. We lived opposite Greylock Mountain in Massachusetts which is the tallest mountain in Massachusetts. In the state. Our house looked out like this does. It's just not that different even though it's completely across the country.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What did I do 30 years ago? Oh I...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: What was I 14? I was just in 4H doing the same thing our 14 year old is doing now. Except milking more cows. Doing the haying and all the things in the garden and the canning and the sewing. Well if I had to I could go back teaching school there would be no problem with that. I used to teach Sunday school but I don't anymore.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is it just a time limitation?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Also I'm not as enthused about the church program right at the present time as I was then. And at that time we were very good friends with the minister's family that was here but that wasn't necessarily the reason I did it. But I did it because I wanted to. Now circumstances have just changed at the church and also if we do too much living as far out as we do it means the kids are trapped at church for a very long time. And that's a bad place for three teenage boys to be and still retain any desire to go to church or Sunday school or anything else if you expect them to stay too long. So we don't want to wreck that. So our church involvement has been much less. However our children's church activities have increased recently. Last year first the two youngest ones and then all of them. I guess it was the first and third one. First and then all of them got in the Nazarene Church's music program because they have an outstanding music program. So they were going to Sunday school one place, going to the music program the other and then they put on an ecumenical musical, Cool in the Furnace, which was really tremendous. So our whole Sunday was really tied up with all of these things because they practiced for that in the afternoon.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is there a difference between your church activities now and when you were growing up?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh I sang in the choir and I taught Sunday school then. Guess not. We did more or less the same things. There weren't quite as many different things to do then. It was more the routine things. Sunday school and then church. I think there's more variety. Now there are more youth programs here but our boys are in athletics and you can't do both. Because now Coach likes you to take Thursday afternoon off every single week. And that's when it is at the Presbyterian Church. So it's kind of cut down there but then they do go to the music things. I don't know how anybody that didn't live on a farm could ever prepare themselves to live on one. Without being there. I suppose you could go and look. And garden maybe. But I know one of my main responsibilities is getting everything born. And the only thing you can do is be present at 400 births before you feel you've become at all competent.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh really? You think it takes that long?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I don't know. With the sheep. They have very involved births sometimes.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: The goat had problems this year.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It takes a long time and a lot of experience.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You have all sorts of life stuff then.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Because right now we have the beef cub. I don't know if it's warm enough Kathy. You might have to turn it on hotter. And we have a dairy cow. And we have horses. And lots of sheep and a goat. And pigs and chickens and turkeys. So you know between everything. And when something gets sick the only way you can know what to do is to have been there.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you butcher and eat your own meat?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We have. No we don't do that. We have. Usually one of the neighbors does the butchering because we're sort of chicken. But we help take out all the insides after they kill them and do all of that. But we kill the chickens and that kind of stuff.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you cut and wrap your own meat?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well there's a place here that you can go and they cut and saw and things right while you're there. So that you can tell them exactly what you want done and then wrap it up while you're there. Otherwise you have to have lots of expensive tools in order to do a really good job. So it's possible but we don't go into that. We would if we had to.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What else do you have?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well we do get the newspaper now. Up until the last year we didn't ever get the Spokane paper but now we do. We always get the local one. Magazines we get at farm things like the Idaho Farmer, the Goat Journal and the Montedale Sheep Book. Spokane. Sports Illustrated. And Horse Magazine. I don't think we get anything that's non-agricultural except Sports Illustrated. I don't watch TV except once in a blue moon. But I watch the Today Show when I eat breakfast if I can manage it. So I'll get some news. The school bus comes at 8 o'clock and sometimes that's my luxury. Usually about three days a week I get to watch a little of that.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do the children watch TV much?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Not this time of year. But from say 8 o'clock until 9 in that range sometimes they will sneak something in. But lately we've been working in the garden until 9 when the weather was good. So just eat something and go to bed.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you have any restrictions on what they watch?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Sometimes there is one that you do not watch TV during the day until after supper or something like that. You cannot just sit around and let the whole day go by watching. But I don't censor it too much anymore. I used to more when they were little.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What do you think about the variety of TV shows that are on?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That's kind of hard for me to answer because I watch it such a limited amount myself. Because our oldest one mostly listens to news and sports programs. We don't even look at a whole big variety of things. Some of those sort of family shows that they watch, I see pieces of once in a while. And once in a while they might watch one of those detective type of things. But they are not up late enough to watch movies or anything like that usually. I think a lot of it that I have seen they could just as well leave off. And then our kids read a lot. Sometimes they read and watch TV at the same time so I am not too sure which they are doing. Or they work on their 4-H books and watch. They rarely just sit in here and just watch. Sort of not the thing to do. You should be doing something else. As a reward I let them watch if they shell peas.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: They get to watch big things so it's not such a bad job.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is there anything you might say about being a doctor's wife?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Marriage it doesn't matter. Nobody thinks of you I don't think as a doctor's wife particularly. Because first I was a teacher and people knew me as a teacher before they knew me as a doctor's wife. And then I am just somebody's mother. I don't really feel that I am put in the classification. There is not any big medical society type things that they have in some places. The auxiliary and all this kind of stuff. Fortunately because I don't know when I sandwiched that in. I really don't think that it makes any difference to anybody.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Are there a lot of interruptions in the night? Emergency type things?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We kind of have an agreement with each other. Mike never woke up for the babies and I don't wake up for the telephones. So a lot of times I don't know. Sometimes I do but they take turns. So it's not as regular as it used to be when there were only two doctors. Then there were lots but now.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What type of doctor is he?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Just a general practitioner. So it isn't too bad.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you know your husband before he came out here? Is that why he came out here? Yes. Why did he come out here?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Because he wanted to practice somewhere else and he had looked into lots of different places and this would feel to him.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you make your own soap? Or have you tried that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No. We make just about everything else I think but we haven't done soap. I have a male. I grind all of our wheat and I make all of our bread. Things like that.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I haven't tried soap.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: One of her neighbors has so it sounded interesting.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: It's really hard.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Have you tried that? Yes. I sew a lot. When I can find time. That's my reward if I get something done. Then I can take time to sew. But that's really hard this time of year to get any of that done. I guess everybody else in the family would probably consider horseback riding. Recreation and relaxation. I don't. But everybody else does. I go to be nice once in a while. But that's not a treat for me.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do the children go on their own horses?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Right. They all ride in the North Idaho Endurance Rides and in the 4-inch competitions. We've all been to the district horse show as well as the local one and things like that. They do a lot.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And practice? I mean, I'm not sure. Did you ever consider living in a city?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No. You know how big Plummer is. I lived there for a little while. Plummer certainly is no city. And that was enough. Oh. No, I have to be out where I can dig and have animals and do things. I just never ever even thought of it. Never. Well, once in a blue moon. Living in town would look good to me today when about 30 things have gone wrong. When we don't have any water and everything has to be watered. When you're not on city water, something's always happening. Last spring we got a rock in the water supply. All it was. But in February you have to dig up the whole water system.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you help do that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: So I didn't help dig. But I helped all water and get everything watered and leave things to the creek and all the rest of those things.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you have any other questions? You know a lot about furnishing. Can you fix it?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, I'm no mechanic. Oh. In fact, none of us are. We have to trade with the neighbors for getting things fixed. Oh, I understand.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you mean the east kind of trades your abilities?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Right.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is there any difference that you noticed between the East and the West?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, my father was probably a little bit more independent as far as trading with people, but he had been a farmer and he was born and he died in the same house. So everything was very familiar to him. That was the way it always was. He did his farming and everything with horses. And there was less that had to be done. You couldn't do it by yourself. And so we probably, although there was one family that we did a lot of trading back and forth with, whereas here there are probably three or four families that we trade back and forth with. Did you notice a difference in people? No. I think there's less difference in farm people than there is in probably city people. Farmers are pretty basically the same

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I think. Are there any particularly interesting stories or incidents that have happened in your life with the children or trips or anything like that? No, I think things have gone rather routinely. Of course, when you say routine, it wouldn't be routine to a lot of people.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Right, but I can't think of any particular thing or any particular place. Did you go to your home? No, this was an old, old farmhouse, but we added on the whole front chunk along the whole front end. I keep fixing one piece at a time. I don't think it'll ever be finished. One thing we'd do in our neighborhood in between, there are probably four families. We'd have to count. Once in a while we have gatherings as to what we have on hand. Well, say for instance on hand tools and things like that so that if there was no gas, we could run the rototillers. What does everybody have that they could help themselves with and what could we trade back and forth? What do we have on hand? Are you keeping your basic essentials in your house? When you run out, are you replacing them? Once in a while we have a Sunday meeting with people and just check up on each other as to how we're doing. What

speaker: Speaker 1
words: are you dependent on the store for? Oh, I can go a long, long time without going to

speaker: Speaker 2
words: the store. Let's say detergent. I keep that on hand. I know that's one of the things. Paper goods? Right, like paper towels and things, but you can really do without them for a certain period of time. I know. But detergent and soap is pretty bad to go without. What about things like sugar or honey? All of us have honey stored. That's one of the things that maybe... Do you have bee hives? No, but that's one of the things that we're trading with. One of the people that we're the closest to has bees. We have the milk cow. Depending upon our land and the amount of resources and things we have, we try to complement what the others have. He's a mechanic. The husband in that family is a mechanic. That's what his trading ability is. That sounds like the way to live. Besides it, there's a lot of things that we do for each other that you can't put a money value on. You just have to figure you have to give your time, which is more valuable

speaker: Speaker 1
words: lots of times. What about carpentry and things like that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Everybody pretty much attacks it the best they can. We had the house, that part built on the house, but we have done a lot of it ourselves. Then there's the people that have the bees and the mechanics. Right now, they're building their own house.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I'm kind of nervous about it. I want to make sure that I get the interview on tape.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Then when things are boring, that's my tradable skill. I have helped quite a few of the people in the neighborhood that way.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you do the same? Isn't it with sheep that if their mother won't nurse them and there's a dead lamb that you use the skin off the dead lamb?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Montadale's are really good mothers. We have had sheep for seven years. We have never had a disowned lamb, but we could. We had one who had a dead lamb once and we wanted to give her one. All you do is take a lamb from somebody else and dunk it in the water from the afterbirth. We have never had any trouble with them taking them that way. It's always been very easy to transfer a lamb without going through the skinning process and everything. Just dunk them in warm water and slap them up a little bit. She thinks she had it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you raise the sheep for their wool or meat?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: The kind we have are dual-purpose sheep. They have very high-quality wool, but they're also good meat sheep. The kids show them both ways. Last year, we had a queen-size blanket made for each of the kids with the wool.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you do your own shearing?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Todd does. We used to always have it done, but sheep shearers are very hard to come by now. It's sort of a lost art. An old sheep shearer in the area sold him his equipment and came and showed him how to do it. It's kind of slow, but he gets it done. He considers that his greatest accomplishment.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What do you do with the wool after that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: There's a wool pool in Spokane most years where all the 4-H kids can take their wool and sell it. Other people can too, but they also cater to the children. That's why we had the blankets made last year. The price was so low, the pool did not sell. They said store it until next year. It's bound to go out. We didn't have good storage facilities, so we had blankets made and a coat for Todd. It was more meaningful to them.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Has anyone in your family ever tried processing the wool themselves, spinning it or anything like that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We tanned some sheepskins with the wool on them. We have those in case anyone has ever bed ridden or something. It was an awful lot of work the way we did it. We haven't tried it since. We know a little lady who has taken our wool and has done spinning. She even sent us a sample of cloth this spring. She's moved to Pennsylvania and she still has to send our wool back there because she can't get any of this quality. That was kind of interesting because she showed us all the stages. Every time she does something new or dyes it differently, she sends it. Louise did that for her science fair project too for three years in a row. She did natural dyeing with just plants. This year she won the Grand Award in Spokane and got sent a world-famous Wikipedia. She feels pretty good about that.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do any of your children do any hand work? Embroidery or anything like that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No. By the time they get their chores done, I'll play sports and musical instruments. They're in all the music programs at the school. All of them do science projects and they're afraid to work. We don't have any time. They might be inclined but we live a very scheduled life. Sometimes I think maybe they are missing something for not having the free time but they're the ones who say, I want to do this, this and this. If you sign up to do it, you will finish it. Have you been back to Massachusetts? The kids and I went back since 1973 and spent two weeks but we can't foresee getting her back there. Again, the way things have been going lately, that's before we had milk cow milking. We had her but she didn't start giving milk yet. She's one of the things that really keeps us tied home because Kent has a big milk clientele that he has to take care of. I hope my mother will come out this fall.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: She's thinking of it. Did you go back before then?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I've been back probably every three or four years. Things didn't get quite as complicated. When the kids were little, they weren't going to school. It was easy. If you could find someone to feed everything. We haven't been back together maybe since Kent was six months

speaker: Speaker 1
words: old and he's 13. Do you go on family picnics or anything like that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Once in an extreme blue moon. We're more apt to have people here. Like the 4th of July, we have the neighborhood celebration here. It's always a big picnic type of thing and everybody brings their fireworks, however many or few they have. Then we put them all off together so we have a display. We always have a big Christmas Eve thing.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is that family or family and friends?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Family and friends, right. Once in a while that gets rotated around, but we have a bigger house than lots of people so it often times ends up here. New Year's Eve we always do something so that hopefully we educate the children to have a good time at home rather than think they must go out. During lots of the year, it's almost impossible to schedule anything that everybody can go to at the same time.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What about fishing and hunting?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Mike doesn't fish or hunt at all. The kids do a little. Not very much. We're very proud of Kent. He killed our sheep. He shot. It's the first thing, first live animal you ever shoot must have been scary. They wiggle around a lot. I was amazed. He had taken gun safety at school and he's taking it in 4H and we had let him shoot ground squirrels. It's different I think. That's another thing, that it requires time to go somewhere. In the winter, when hunting season would be on here, that's when they are all playing basketball probably.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you fish? No. Is there anything else about your life that you can think of?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It's hard to think of your own.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you ever get involved with winter sports? No. Splitting?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No. The normal little things. Skated a little. But I didn't like to ski. I always played basketball. I coached basketball.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Have they always had women's basketball teams?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Back East they did. When I came out here to teach, they did in Plummer. They still had one that went from school to school just like the boys did. Now of course it's being revived everywhere. It has only been out here in Plummer for 15 years.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How would you compare your education with your children's up until high school?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: They've had opportunities to do more things. Not specifically because of what the school did in its everyday things. I don't think there's that much difference there. But in the science fair things that our kids have gone to, their trips to Lewiston and their trips to Spokane and they do educational things while they're there. That kind of thing. They are getting a lot more broader outlook on things. Also they've traveled a lot more on their athletic teams. When I was in high school there wasn't a debate team or anything and I think Todd has gained tremendously from going on things like that. Then our music program back East, we just stayed home unless we went to a basketball game or something in a very nearby town because the town is back there is very close, like six miles or something. Whereas when our kids go, they might go 150 miles just to play at a basketball game. The music program had a trip to Southern Idaho this year. The debate team went to Boise. The science fair kids went to Lewiston and Spokane. So they have traveled a great deal more than I ever did while I was going to school.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What do you think about a lot of the new ideas in education?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I think that they're alright, especially for the kids who aren't having any trouble in just the basic things. It's harder for them to adjust to the changes and things if things aren't pretty repetitious from one year to another. But for the rest of them it's probably fine. I used to worry that, especially in this area, that all the emphasis and extra money was spent on handicapped children and slow learners and things. They really have very few programs for fast students or anything, for accelerated ones. But if you get involved in culture, music and debate and all the rest of those things, you don't have time for any of that anyway. In a small town like this, it's the same kids who do everything. It isn't spread out as much. Because I know the science teacher was complaining when they have to compete in Spokane, they said the good science students in Spokane are scientists and they're science students. But here they're the same kids who are playing on the basketball team and playing in the band and everything else. Because there are so few kids for so many things. Those kids probably wouldn't even make the basketball team. They'd have more time to spend on it. Anyway, I don't have any complaints about it. I'm a regular attender of school board meetings once in a while. I cause quite a disturbance over things. When did you get a sense out? The building of the school. Because I was chairman of the bond committee. The bond was passed in December of 1973 and they still haven't dug a hole. Do you like the location that's planned? I liked the previous location better. This one is handy, it's closer to us, but I think it has a lot less of desirable features. They spent a whole year and a half fighting over that. They changed the location three times. It makes no kind of sense because we have lost so much to inflation and building costs. I just feel they should have gone ahead and done what they said they were going to do. Did you get involved in politics? No, just school politics. I had to get riled up in order to get involved in political things. I felt very involved in that. And then the school is so overcrowded that they're using almost every church in town to hold school. So as a regular everyday basis, next year they won't have to use the Fernwood one anymore because the new Fernwood grade school has finished. This year they'll be using the Presbyterian and Lutheran churches every single day. They were using one of the other churches until it was sold for the special education program and now they had to sandwich that in somewhere. To have the bond passed and not do anything for the Presbyterian. I hope they don't have a gas shortage before our kids get out of school. But it's not getting to school and back that's our problem. It's all the extracurricular things. Last year I drove 28 miles a day just getting everyone to basketball practice and back.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Are there anyone else out here that you...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: One family. We do take turns with our junior high age ones. Yeah. So however in September Todd should be able to get his license and then we have an old jeep that he can take part of the time and that will help. From the time they get home from school all I do is get people where they go either to music lessons or athletic events or taking acrobats, dancing. We're lucky the music teacher lives down around the corner from us so in good weather or in daylight they can walk.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What type of... Is it singing or do they also play instruments?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, they all play instruments.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you ever get together and have them play as a family thing?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well we try to usually do that at Christmas but it gets very complicated because one plays in the grade school band, one in the junior high and two in the high school and it is very difficult to get music that coordinates everybody on their correct level. However a man came last, maybe two weeks ago and is interested in buying a horse from us and he is taking music composition down at the University of Idaho for his master's degree. So that's one of the things he thought would be fun to do is be to write some music for us. So that may materialize.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Sounds good.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We have one musical child, the rest of them just sort of manage.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Have you all put the experience on that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I have always felt it was a very good discipline so whether you had any talent or not you would fight it out with the instrument. And then I always read the articles to the kids on how if you teach your hands and your mind to work on a musical instrument it will increase your athletic ability and of course it has great appeal to boys. And there are some statistics on that. So for those reasons as well as for the pleasure that people usually derive from it as they get older, we thought music was very important.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How did they feel about letting you have fun?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh each boy made a shirt and they didn't complain at all.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did the high schools here have home experiments for boys?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I think they do now but with everything else they are doing they could never fit it in anyway.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah. Besides they don't need it right?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Right. Because they have all had at least four years of cooking in 4-H. And they can do some basic sewing. And there is no way they can get out of helping when you are canning or dehydrating or something. Everybody has to help. We made jerky out of a whole lamb last year so they got a lot of practice making jerky.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you smoke that or just use your dehydrator?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We just use the dehydrator. We marinate it and then put it in there.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Anything else? Nothing. I don't want to make you late. It's about 10 after 12.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Right. I don't have to wait until quarter of one. And I think everybody is packed. I think I got everybody cleaned before you got here. So what do you think to do about this stuff now that I have a minute so I can listen?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: At present I will be taking these back. We will take all the recorders and cassettes to reel to reel. And it will probably be stored at the Women's Center until November. And that's when the money for the grant, or that's when the grant is over. They may decide to provide another grant so that they can do some writing and editing. And the editing would be just like where you talked about, where you learned about child rearing. We mark the footage and that sort of thing. And if the grant doesn't do anything else it will be in the archives and then I will give you the release form. Researchers could go and use it. If your children wanted to go and watch them for some time, it will be available for them. And probably it would be there mostly for researchers and relatives.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That is a fun thing I bet for you.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh it is. I believe in St. Mary's as a friendly town. I have met really wonderful people here. And I think the happiest people I have ever met on the whole have been here. Just to pick up their enthusiasm about life and the way that they are living and being satisfied with their life.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That's good. I have felt it's a good place for the kids. School isn't fancy. They don't provide lots of things. One of my sister's children go to school in Syracuse, New York, which is big and it's a university town and everything. But I wouldn't trade the educational advantages to the just plain living advantages here.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But I think your children are learning so much.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I'm just real satisfied.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Just doing things and that's the most important thing in life.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Right. They learn to do many more things other than just study. I think where it's the city things. There's more emphasis on the book education. They have some very fine teachers I think here. There are those that you're not so impressed with but that happens no matter where you are. And if a kid is interested in that particular thing they'll learn it anyway. Provided they know how to read.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I was thinking at the Women's Center we have a brown bag series and a focus series. And the focus series is something where we will have a continuing thing like marriage and alternatives. And we have a panel of married couples and a panel of couples who are living together. Some people talking about divorces separated or widows and that sort of thing. Or we have lawyers come in and talk about all sorts of things. Things that deal with women. But would you be interested in sometime just coming up and talking about the life of a little woman. It's usually at noon and it would be sometime during the winter. Do you think that we could plan on something like that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It's kind of scary to think about. But I'm convinced. About October and November are months that I can sometimes foresee leaving home.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I don't know what is already scheduled yet. But I think it would be really fantastic to have you come and talk. And there's usually, oh it just depends. It changes from year to year. I remember when you came last year I think it was kind of slack. And from what I heard the year before they had a lot of people come in at noon. And so there would be people asking questions and things like that. And it's a very relaxed atmosphere. I think you'd probably be relaxed anyway. But it is. And could we kind of plan on maybe?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I wouldn't say no now because I could say something I'm convinced of. And it's something that well even in like our own neighborhood and through our forage things we're, I really feel it's necessary for people to get more down to earth and be less dependent on stores and transportation. There are a lot of little things that if people know, it's not that hard. But if you don't know you're lost.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Have you heard about Carla Emory?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I have looked through her book. I haven't, the other people have had. I have a big collection of books from the inflation survival people. And so far I haven't decided that I needed her because of what I've had. However, every once in a while I think about it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, you probably never have to go anywhere as far.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: So a lot of it is practical things that I, I wonder if she's accumulated any more information than I grew up with. Because a lot of these things she had learned since she came here.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, the latest book is something that I think a lot of people who are working with at school have written. It's just different survival things. And one of the men has written a book on energy. And I haven't seen that. I've just gotten the information on it.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Our oldest boy is especially interested in the survival foods and things long before it became a big thing. He was still in grade school when he did his science project on wild and poisonous, edible and poisonous plants in the area. In fact I have to pick it up. It's at the library now, his display. And he studied it at the University of Idaho when he went down to that 4-H thing that they have for close congress. And he's done a lot with that. He wants to be a landscape architect. So he's really interested in plants. We're into our first year. And of course the weather has been so abnormal this year that it's difficult to tell. However, we did know that peas and onions didn't like each other. And we planted them together because we thought we'd pull the peas after they were mature and the onions would still be there. And then we found out they didn't like each other. And the peas are doing great. But the onions are terrible. And we have had in the past a difficult time with cucumbers. And it seems to be typical of this area. Cucumbers do not germinate well and they don't do well. And we planted them in the row where sunflowers had been last year. And we planted sunflowers in with them this year. And we had fantastic cucumbers. Every seed came up. So we don't know. We'll have to do it more than once before we know. Kent? Where did you get your information for your demonstration?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What are your sources of information? Nicholas Gardner's pamphlet, the Organic Gardening magazine, and how to grow more vegetables in your flat plot.
